title: How to NOT Freak Out about the Common Core
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart diagnoses the two common teacher reactions to the Common Core, fighting it or avoiding it, as brain-stem fight-or-flight responses from educators already overloaded by parents, deadlines, IEPs and testing. His counterproposal, the 'non-freaked out approach', is to choose two or three standards a team judges most important for college and career readiness and deliberately ignore the rest until those are mastered. He grounds this in Mike Schmoker's Focus, arguing that even the leaner Common Core holds far too much to become excellent at all at once, and that standards imposed wholesale merely garnish lesson plans. He recasts fight-or-flight productively: flee from all but the most important standards and fight the pressure to master everything now. The practical center is a fifteen-minute protocol his social studies PLC used to settle on close reading (R.CCR.1) and text-based argument (W.CCR.1), followed by experimenting, sharing results and discussing. The payoff he claims is ownership: the team now owns standards it once had not even read.
points: Stuart reads teachers' two dominant responses to the Common Core - resistance and avoidance - as fight-or-flight reactions to overload rather than considered positions.
His core move is deliberate neglect: focus on two or three high-leverage standards, master them, and only then move on, treating purposeful ignoring as the professional choice.
He argues that standards imposed all at once only garnish lesson plans, so teachers should fight pressure to 'master them all now' with Schmoker's Focus in hand.
The article supplies a concrete fifteen-minute PLC protocol: read the twenty anchor standards, each pick the neediest reading and writing standard, and reach consensus.
His department's choice of close reading and text-based argument illustrates the payoff he claims - a team moving from never having read the standards to owning them.
quotes: And when something like the Common Core State Standards (CCSS) come out, our frontal lobes, already overwhelmed by parents and deadlines and IEPs and ACTs and AYP, delegate to our brain stems, and our brain stems immediately shift us into fight-or-flight mode.
Once you've chosen the most crucial standards, it's empowerment time: ignore the rest of them while you, your students, and your colleagues work on dominating the few you chose.

In my professional opinion, the only way to sensibly use these standards is to focus on a few, master them, and, only when mastered, move on from there. Bluntly, the professional thing to do is start by purposefully ignoring a majority of the CCSS. We should not be moving on to new things when we haven't yet demonstrably mastered the most important, basic things.
Seriously: standards are pointless if they merely garnish lesson plans, and that's all they will do if we give in to unreasonable pressures that say, “Master them all now.

In short: apply both flight and fight modes to the CCSS; fly from all but the most important, and fight pressures that tell you otherwise. Take the standards and make them meaningful for your setting.

The process for choosing where to start with the CCSS took our building's social studies professional learning community (PLC) about 15 minutes. When we began the process below, most of us had never read a word of the CCSS before.
Why? Because instead of being freaked out by the CCSS, our PLC now owns them. We've made them manageable and meaningful to us and our goals for our students.
